Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2606.15982v1 [cs.CV] 14 Jun 2026 Mind the Gap: Diagnosing Constraint Discovery Failures in Text-in-Image Editing Rui Gui Abstract A key challenge in multimodal reasoning is determining which visual dependencies become relevant under a specific task, rather than merely recognizing visible content. We study this through edit-induced constraint discovery in text-in-image editing, a controlled diagnostic setting where a local text change can activate secondary consistency constraints: given a valid editing instruction and an image, can a model identify the secondary regions that must also change? Across 461 diagnostic cases, four MLLMs, and 19 constraint subtypes, models recover only 46% case-level macro recall under unguided prompting versus 94% when constraints are explicitly provided—suggesting that a substantial portion of the failure arises when models must decide which unstated dependencies to surface. Oracle-field decomposition shows that case-specific causal explanations are the most effective partial guidance (0.782 recall), above region names (0.610) or type labels (0.646), suggesting that edit-specific causal cues account for much of the oracle gain. A downstream experiment further shows that higher self-discovery recall does not necessarily improve task performance: unverified self-discovery introduces false positives that offset recall gains, motivating precision-aware constraint elicitation. Central South University Introduction Many multimodal tasks require models to surface task-relevant but unstated visual dependencies—conditions that are not mentioned in the instruction yet must be satisfied for a correct response. Recent MLLMs excel at visual understanding ( Hurst et al. 2024 ; Comanici et al. 2025 ; Liu et al. 2023 ; Alayrac et al. 2022 ) , yet they often fail to discover such dependencies spontaneously in task-driven settings. Text-in-image editing provides a controlled diagnostic setting for this problem: a local text change can activate secondary consistency constraints elsewhere in the image (e.g., changing a discount should also update the derived price) ( Gui et al. 2025 ) . Our diagnostic evaluates whether MLLMs can explicitly identify edit-induced dependencies under a controlled elicitation interface, not downstream image generation. This isolates an upstream source of failure: the same models can often identify the relevant dependency when it is made explicit, but do not surface it spontaneously. Consider a promotional poster showing “50% OFF” alongside a price tag of “$50.” When instructed to change the discount to “30% OFF,” an MLLM may correctly identify the need to revise the discount text but leave the price tag unchanged—despite the mathematical relationship linking them. Similarly, changing text near a reflective surface should trigger an update to its reflection, and modifying a label on a symmetric structure should update the corresponding label on the other side. These are implicit constraints : conditions not stated in the editing instruction but reasonably expected to hold after the edit, arising from physical, spatial, semantic, stylistic, or cross-modal dependencies. The relevant knowledge is nonetheless accessible: when constraints are made explicit through our oracle conditions, the same models recognize and verify 94% of these dependencies—much of the failure appears to lie in surfacing them spontaneously when reasoning about the edit. We call this a discovery failure : the task of recognizing which secondary elements are affected by a given edit ( edit-induced constraint discovery ) is not triggered, and models default to specifying only the local text replacement without considering broader consequences. Work on latent knowledge ( Burns et al. 2022 ; Yan et al. 2025 ) suggests models can hold information they do not spontaneously express. This prior work motivates our diagnostic framing; the empirical claims below rest on the measured discovery–verification gap. The measured gap is also heterogeneous: unguided recall varies 2.7 × 2.7\times across constraint categories (and 6.3 × 6.3\times across the finer subtypes). To study this, we introduce the Implicit Constraint Graph (ICG), a structured annotation schema that makes explicit the edit-induced constraints triggered by an editing instruction (Figure 1 ). Unlike scene graphs ( Johnson et al. 2015 ; Krishna et al. 2017 ; Zellers et al. 2018 ; Chang et al. 2021 ) that capture pre-existing objects, attributes, and relationships, or visual grounding approaches ( Yang et al. 2023a ; Peng et al. 2024 ) that localize existing image regions, ICG represents editing-induced constraints: how changing element A A should cascade to elements B B and C C . Each constraint node specifies an affected region, its dependency reason, constraint type, and expected update; optional inter-node edges capture consistency requirements among affected regions. We design a controlled diagnostic framework with seven prompting conditions (Figure 2 ) spanning no guidance (Direct) to full oracle provision. Adversarial, E inter E_{\text{inter}} ablation, and oracle-field decomposition controls then test whether the oracle gain reflects case-specific causal constraint information, inter-node consistency edges, or blind compliance. We evaluate 461 cases across four strong contemporary MLLMs, covering 19 constraint subtypes in five categories: Physical, Spatial, Semantic, Style, and Cross-modal. Our experiments yield three main findings: 1. Discovery failure is structured. Unguided recall varies 2.7 × 2.7\times across constraint categories, from cross-modal to semantic constraints; finer subtype-level variation ( 6.3 × 6.3\times ) is larger but exploratory. 2. Case-specific causal information is the strongest partial oracle cue. The E inter E_{\text{inter}} ablation ( Δ = + 0.007 \Delta=+0.007 ) and adversarial control (90.5% rejection) argue against inter-node edges or blind compliance as primary explanations. By contrast, oracle-field decomposition shows that de-identified causal explanations (0.782 recall) outperform region names (0.610) and type labels (0.646), indicating that edit-specific dependency reasons account for a large part of the oracle guidance. 3. Higher discovery recall does not automatically improve downstream use. A downstream experiment shows that NL-Self’s +0.155 recall gain over Direct yields no plan-satisfaction improvement ( d = − 0.05 d=-0.05 , p = 0.62 p=0.62 ), because unverified self-discovery introduces false positives that offset recall gains. In summary, we contribute: (1) an edit-induced constraint discovery formulation and structured annotation schema (19 subtypes, 5 categories); (2) a controlled diagnostic framework with seven prompting conditions plus oracle-field decomposition (Region/Reason/Type-Only), separating discovery from verification; (3) an empirical characterization of where discovery fails and which oracle information helps, with adversarial, format, and decomposition controls; and (4) evidence that higher discovery recall alone does not improve downstream use, motivating precision-aware constraint elicitation. Figure 1: Example ICG annotation for an aircraft rebranding edit. Changing the fuselage airline name triggers three constraint nodes spanning two categories (semantic and style). The tail logo ( n 1 n_{1} ) must match the new brand identity, the livery colors ( n 2 n_{2} ) must adopt the target airline’s palette, and secondary markings ( n 3 n_{3} ) must maintain visual coherence. Edges indicate edit-target-to-region dependencies and optional consistency relations among affected regions. Related Work Text-in-Image Editing and Evaluation. Diffusion-based methods improve text rendering and local text editing ( Tuo et al. 2024 ; Chen et al. 2023 ; Yang et al. 2023b ) , while instruction-based and MLLM-guided editors use natural-language or multimodal guidance to produce better edited images ( Brooks et al. 2023 ; Zhang et al. 2023a ; Basu et al. 2023 ; Fu et al. 2024 ; Huang et al. 2024 ; Yin et al. 2025 ) . Editing benchmarks evaluate final outputs under fidelity, instruction following, preservation, or reasoning-aware criteria ( Zhao et al. 2026 ; Liu et al. 2026 ; Yosef et al. 2025 ; Ma et al. 2024 ; Yi et al. 2026 ; Ding et al. 2026 ; Lin et al. 2026 ; Wang et al. 2025 ) . In contrast, we use editing instructions as controlled probes: our object of evaluation is not the edited image, but whether an MLLM can explicitly identify unmentioned visual dependencies activated by an instruction-image pair. Structured Prompting and Visual Dependency Reasoning. CoT and decomposed or graph-structured prompting can improve reasoning but have mixed effects in visual tasks ( Wei et al. 2022 ; Zhang et al. 2023c ; Shao et al. 2024 ; Izadi et al. 2026 ; Khot et al. 2022 ; Besta et al. 2024 ) ; visual grounding and scene representations localize or encode existing objects and relations ( Yang et al. 2023a ; Peng et al. 2024 ; Johnson et al. 2015 ; Krishna et al. 2017 ; Zellers et al. 2018 ; Chang et al. 2021 ; Shen et al. 2025 ) . Our setting differs because the relevant dependencies are instruction-conditioned: a secondary region matters only because a particular edit would make it inconsistent with the target. Implicit Reasoning and Problem Detection. Work on latent knowledge and elicitation shows that model behavior can change with how information is queried ( Burns et al. 2022 ) . Most closely related, HiPS ( Yan et al. 2025 ) shows that MLLMs often comply with flawed instructions rather than surface hidden problems. Our instructions are valid; the challenge is instead to identify secondary dependencies that the request implicitly activates. Related failures in semantic fixation and constraint satisfaction further motivate studying when models fail to surface task-relevant information ( Alam 2026 ; Kovalev et al. 2025 ; Huang et al. 2023 ) . Method Problem Formulation Given an image I I and an editing instruction T T , an implicit constraint is a condition c c that is (1) not explicitly stated in T T , (2) arises from visual, semantic, physical, or stylistic dependencies between the edited element and other elements in I I , and (3) would reasonably be expected to hold after the edit. Our goal is to diagnose whether an MLLM can identify all implicit constraints triggered by ( I , T ) (I,T) . Edit-Induced Constraint Annotation Schema We define a structured annotation schema for edit-induced constraints, represented as G ⁡ ( V , E edit , E inter ) G(V,E_{\text{edit}},E_{\text{inter}}) : • V = { n 1 , … , n k } V=\{n_{1},\ldots,n_{k}\} : Constraint nodes, each representing a region implicitly affected by the edit. Each n i n_{i} carries attributes: spatial region r i r_{i} , constraint type τ i ∈ 𝒯 \tau_{i}\in\mathcal{T} , expected update u i u_{i} , and dependency reason d i d_{i} (why this region is affected). • E edit E_{\text{edit}} : Edges from the edit target to each affected node, encoding the edit-induced dependency. • E inter E_{\text{inter}} : Optional edges capturing consistency requirements between affected nodes. This representation separates four pieces of diagnostic information: the affected region, the constraint type, the expected update, and the reason the edit propagates there. Optional inter-node edges record consistency relations among affected regions. Constraint Taxonomy We organize implicit constraints into 5 categories with 19 subtypes (Table 1 ). Categories are informed by scene graph modeling ( Krishna et al. 2017 ) , controllable generation ( Zhang et al. 2023b ) , and perceptual organization theory ( Treisman and Gelade 1980 ; Greff et al. 2020 ) ; subtypes were stabilized through iterative pilot annotation until no new type appeared in five consecutive cases (details in supplementary). The taxonomy was finalized before case selection from non-TextEditBench sources (Pexels, Unsplash, Canva), reducing circularity for the newly collected portion; TextEditBench overlap is addressed by source-stratified analyses in the supplementary material. The full taxonomy with descriptions and examples appears in the supplementary material. Category Subtype N N Physical Reflection / Shadow 79 Perspective / Occlusion 89 Spatial Mirror / Symmetry 32 Repetition 24 Semantic Numerical 19 Categorical / Functional 75 Promotional / Visual-Data 72 Style Font / Color / Layout / Material 173 Cross-modal Scene / Temporal / Cultural 213 Total 776 Figure 2: Diagnostic framework overview. Each case (image + editing instruction) is evaluated under seven prompting conditions spanning no guidance to full oracle. Model responses are scored against the ground-truth ICG by an automated judge, yielding per-constraint recall and precision. Two ablation conditions (Adversarial, Oracle-NoInter) and three oracle-field decomposition conditions (Region-Only, Reason-Only, Type-Only) provide additional control evidence. A downstream planning evaluation further tests whether discovery improvements translate into better edit plans (plan satisfaction). Diagnostic Pipeline Stage 1: Constraint Elicitation. Given ( I , T ) (I,T) , the model identifies implicit constraints. Under ICG-Self, the model outputs a structured JSON graph; under ICG-Oracle, the human-annotated graph is provided. Stage 2: Response Formation. The model reports discovered constraints or, under oracle conditions, uses provided constraints to formulate the required updates. Stage 3: Evaluation. An automated judge compares the model’s output against the ground-truth ICG to measure constraint recall. We focus on Stage 1 (constraint discovery) as the primary diagnostic target. This pipeline is an evaluation decomposition for diagnosing constraint discovery; it does not assume that real editing systems have an explicit planning stage with this architecture. Adversarial Oracle Control. To measure acceptance bias under oracle prompting, we inject one plausible but factually incorrect constraint per case alongside the ground-truth constraints. Models must label each constraint as VALID or INVALID. E inter E_{\text{inter}} Ablation. We compare ICG-Oracle (full graph) against Oracle-NoInter (same nodes and E edit E_{\text{edit}} , with only E inter E_{\text{inter}} removed) on the 228 cases containing inter-constraint dependencies. Experimental Setup Data Construction We curate 461 diagnostic cases, each consisting of an image I I , an editing instruction T T , and a human-annotated ground-truth ICG with 776 total constraint nodes (1.68 per case on average). Images are sourced from TextEditBench ( Gui et al. 2025 ) , Pexels, Unsplash, and Canva (filtered by automated pre-screening). Underrepresented subtypes were supplemented with additional cases collected from other sources to ensure coverage. Candidate selection uses a three-stage protocol: (1) automated pre-screening by Claude Opus 4.6; (2) human inspection of visual quality; (3) final review of complete annotations. Each constraint node must have its affected region visibly present in the image and be based on direct observation rather than assumption. Annotation quality. Three annotators with computer-science backgrounds independently classified a stratified sample of 60 nodes: Fleiss’ κ = 0.77 \kappa=0.77 (substantial; details in the supplementary material). An independent verification audit on a 20 % 20\% stratified sample of all 776 nodes (156 nodes) checks existence, region correctness, update correctness, and reason validity; per-dimension agreement ranges from 84.6% to 90.4% across four dimensions (details in the supplementary material). This audit complements the subtype-classification agreement above by showing that the affected region, expected update, and dependency reason are also largely supported by an independent verifier. Models We evaluate Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-4o ( Hurst et al. 2024 ) , Gemini 2.5 Flash ( Comanici et al. 2025 ) , and Qwen3-VL-Plus ( Bai et al. 2025 ) —spanning four major commercial model families (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Alibaba). All use temperature = 0 =0 and max_tokens = 4096 =4096 (Gemini: 16384 under CoT). Images standardized to 1024px max long edge. The automated judge is Claude Sonnet 4.6; adversarial constraints are generated by GPT-4o for independence from the Claude judge family. Experimental Conditions We test each case under seven prompting conditions (Figure 2 ): Direct (no guidance), CoT (step-by-step), ICG-Self (JSON graph output), NL-Self (free-form, same information dimensions), Signal-Guided (a free-form prompt that directs models to inspect common high-risk cues such as repeated text, reflections, shadows, prices, charts, and brand/style consistency, without providing case-specific affected regions), Taxonomy-Only (19-subtype checklist, no case-specific nodes), and ICG-Oracle (ground-truth constraints provided); plus ICG-Adversarial (oracle + one injected invalid constraint), Oracle-NoInter (oracle without E inter E_{\text{inter}} edges), and three oracle-field decomposition conditions: Region-Only (affected regions without type or reason), Reason-Only (de-identified causal explanations without region names), and Type-Only (constraint type labels only). Full prompts appear in the supplementary material. Evaluation An automated judge (Claude Sonnet 4.6) evaluates whether each ground-truth constraint was identified, requiring the response to identify the affected region, state that it needs to be updated, and give a dependency reason matching the ground-truth constraint. In this work, “discovery” refers not merely to naming an affected region, but to producing a minimally actionable constraint: the region, the need for an update, and the causal link to the edit. The largest partial gain comes from supplying the causal relation linking the edit to affected regions. Discussion From Discovery to Downstream Use: Recall Gains Require Precision. A natural assumption is that helping models discover more constraints will directly improve edit plans. We test this with a planning experiment (60 stratified cases, 100 constraints, 3 conditions; protocol in the supplementary material). Providing ground-truth constraints yields near-perfect plan satisfaction (0.990); unguided Direct prompting drops to 0.700 ( Δ = 0.29 \Delta=0.29 , p < 10 − 8 p<10^{-8} ), confirming that missed constraints degrade planning. Crucially, however, NL-Self—which achieves +0.155 higher discovery recall than Direct—shows no improvement in plan satisfaction (0.680 vs. 0.700; Δ = − 0.02 \Delta=-0.02 , Cohen’s d = − 0.05 d=-0.05 , p = 0.62 p=0.62 ). The effect, if anything, is slightly negative. This dissociation arises because planning quality depends on precision as well as recall: NL-Self’s broader search surfaces additional true constraints but also introduces false positives that generate unnecessary edit steps, offsetting the recall benefit. A two-stage discover-then-verify variant also remains well short of Oracle (0.712), suggesting that post-hoc filtering alone may not compensate for unreliable initial discovery. 2 2 2 The two-stage pipeline reaches 0.712 plan satisfaction on a related 58-case run after filtering 31.2% of candidate constraints; full setup and comparability caveat are in the supplementary material. This motivates precision-aware constraint elicitation: closing the discovery gap requires not just broader search but surfacing the right constraints without flooding the plan with spurious ones. Implications for Multimodal Reasoning and Editing Systems. We interpret this pattern as a knowledge-deployment gap in this setting: models can often apply or verify the relevant relational knowledge once it is explicitly cued (evidenced by high Oracle recall) but do not reliably activate it from the editing instruction alone. This gap may be relevant to other multimodal tasks requiring task-activated dependency reasoning, although our evidence is specific to text-in-image editing. For editing-oriented applications, these results motivate explicit dependency elicitation as a useful diagnostic or auxiliary step: a model first proposes candidate secondary changes grounded in visible regions and dependency reasons, which can then be verified before use. Cross-Family Generalization. A preliminary open-weight check (GLM-4.6V on a 50-case stratified subset) shows the same qualitative pattern: Direct recall 0.388 rises to Oracle recall 0.970 (gap + 0.582 +0.582 ), within the proprietary range. A single model on 50 cases is suggestive rather than conclusive. Limitations. Our 461 cases cover all 19 subtypes with N ≥ 14 N\geq 14 , but several remain below 25, limiting per-subtype ranking stability. The primary judge (Claude Sonnet 4.6) shares lineage with one evaluated model, but two additional judges—GPT-4o ( κ = 0.617 \kappa=0.617 – 0.646 0.646 ) and out-of-pool DeepSeek ( κ = 0.598 \kappa=0.598 – 0.698 0.698 )—both reproduce the Direct → \rightarrow Oracle gap. Same-family judging is therefore a mitigated source of uncertainty rather than a driver of the headline result. Candidate pre-screening used Claude Opus 4.6; a source-stratified analysis shows Claude’s Direct recall is actually lower on pre-screened cases (0.590) than on other sources (0.679–0.681), providing no support for a pre-screening bias. The downstream experiment evaluates text-based edit plans rather than final generated images; end-to-end generation evaluation remains future work. Our study is a behavioral diagnostic of language-mediated constraint discovery; it does not claim to reveal the internal latent representations used by end-to-end generation models. Conclusion We introduced edit-induced constraint discovery as a diagnostic task for task-activated visual dependency reasoning, instantiated in text-in-image editing. Across 461 cases and four MLLMs, models achieve less than half of secondary consistency recall under unguided prompting but recover most constraints when those dependencies are made explicit. The gap is not uniform: it varies by constraint type and is largest for dependencies requiring weak edit cues, cross-region search, or external knowledge. Oracle-field decomposition shows that case-specific causal descriptions provide the strongest partial guidance, while a downstream experiment shows that recall gains alone are insufficient when self-discovery also introduces false positives. These results suggest that task-activated dependency discovery is a distinct bottleneck in multimodal reasoning, and that effective constraint elicitation requires precision as well as recall.
